speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Mr Chairman, Sir, I beg to move, "That the total sum to be allocated for Head M of the Estimates be reduced by $100".

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In business budgeting, this phenomenon is known as the negative draw, that is, when the rate of growth in expenditures exceeds the rate of growth in revenue.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: If left unchecked, where expenditures continue to grow faster than revenues, we could end up with a ballooning deficit situation in the years to come.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Otherwise, our Budgets will run into structural deficits.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Thirdly, both the short‐term recurring expenditures as well as the long-term infrastructure spending have grown larger and are projected to increase further in the decades ahead.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In particular, social and healthcare spending will rise as our population enters into a faster pace of ageing and healthcare needs increase further.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In his Budget Statement speech, the Finance Minister spoke about pursuing differentiated fiscal strategy to fund our various spending, namely, one approach for major infrastructural investments, and another for recurrent social and security expenditures.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I agree with the Finance Minister that for recurrent spending like healthcare, security and other social expenditures where it directly benefits the current generation, they should be funded with current taxation so that every generation pays its share.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This approach would also instil the spending discipline as any further rise in recurring expenditures would have to be funded through more taxes.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This in‐built discipline will not only help keep our operating Budget sustainable but also fairer as well across generations.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: For long-term mega infrastructure projects with high capital outlays, the Government should, as far as possible, set aside surpluses where possible, to use the savings accumulated to pay part of the lumpy investment, which is what we have been doing in the past.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This pre‐funding approach demonstrates commitment and ensures that there is sufficient funding for projects with very high capital expenditures, such as the Cross Island Mass Rapid Transit (MRT) Line.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: But I also agree with the Finance Minister that with the new financing approach for projects, especially where they generate future economic returns, and those that are long-term in nature with some uncertainty, the entity that undertakes the project can look to borrow to finance the project and potentially could draw on the Government's guarantee to lower the financing costs of these long-term borrowings.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The Government is a net creditor and actually does not need to borrow other than the issuance of Singapore Government Securities, which is there to help create a risk-free bond market yield curve.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: However, for the entity that builds the Government-invested infrastructure, borrowing at the project level does require higher financing costs because of the risks associated, such as construction risks.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This could result in a negative carry situation from the Government's standpoint where the borrowing rates may be higher than the returns from investing the Reserves.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Hence, it makes smart sense to tap on Government guarantee to reduce the borrowing costs.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I have a few questions for the Finance Minister.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Thirdly, as I have said earlier, our investment income from our Reserves is now a significant source of Government revenue.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: How does the Government ensure that we will not be overly reliant on it, especially as the investment climate is getting more volatile?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: And finally, in the midst of changing to this new approach, how do we also ensure that our tax regime remains progressive, with the higher-income earners shouldering more of the tax burden?

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: This high dependency represents a significant vulnerability, given the volatility of any investment portfolio.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Experts are divided on how much risk corporate taxes – this is traditionally Singapore's largest source of revenue – pose to Singapore's fiscal sustainability.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Most agree that it will be increasingly difficult to raise corporate taxes, especially as major economies, such as the United States (US) lower them.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Personal income taxes are also expected to contribute less to revenue in the coming years, due to our greying population.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Our ageing population will further demand higher spending in healthcare and to build elderly-friendly infrastructure.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: So, to pay for our increasing needs, I urge the Government to study all possible streams of revenue, with the Goods and Services Tax (GST) rate as a last resort, given its broad impact on society.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Could the Government look instead at introducing e-commerce tax, a lift in gambling, tobacco and alcohol taxes, perhaps new sources of tax revenue from carbon and sugar, and more progressive personal income tax by introducing new and higher tax brackets, including those for the super high-income earners and ultra-rich?

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: So, to address the fiscal sustainability, perhaps we can also balance this with more focus on the "costs" line.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: It is always easy to call on the Government to do more and give more, usually with less consideration on how these expenditures are going to be paid for.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: So, I would like to ask the Finance Minister about the process by which large projects and programmes are prioritised, and whether Singaporeans can play a bigger role in influencing this process, so that they can feel included in the building of Singapore.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The size of the fund GIC manages has been estimated by some at well over hundreds of billions of dollars.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: GIC's latest report states that the reason for this decline is that the high returns from the beginning of the tech bubble window have dropped out of the rolling 20-year return window while the post-tech bubble declines have remained.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: GIC foresees this decline in the rolling 20-year annualised rate of return to continue for a few years, although the same report states that, in most recent years, the returns have been good.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In previous replies in Parliament on fund performance, officeholders have stated that the Government's view is that GIC and Temasek have performed creditably in challenging market conditions.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: How does the Government ascertain this beyond the inputs of individuals who are on the boards of these funds?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: How does the public scrutinise fund performance and comparison to other fund managers with not too dissimilar or long-term mandates?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: What does the GIC mean when it states the returns from the recent years have been good?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: And what is stopping the fund from reporting its yearly performance so as to meaningfully allow the public to track its performance closely, as we see with Temasek today?

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Mr Chairman, tax structure has an important role to play in retirement adequacy.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: We grant income tax reliefs for retirement savings, and we do not tax income from retirement accounts, except for the Supplementary Retirement Scheme (SRS) at a concessionary rate.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: These tax advantages are a hidden subsidy to retirement for the rich.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Because the value of tax relief depends on Assessable Income, high-income Singaporeans benefit much more than the low-income do.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: The Minister stated recently that 90% of those making SRS contributions have Assessable Income above $80,000, and the average marginal tax rate there is about 15% for those making the contributions.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: As for Central Provident Fund (CPF), my estimates suggest that CPF tax reliefs cost the Treasury about $1 billion annually.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: We might accept this if tax relief was effective at increasing retirement savings.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: A review by Bernatzi et al, published in Psychological Science in 2017, suggests tax incentives only generate a few dollars of incremental retirement savings for each tax dollar spent.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: This is an order of magnitude less cost‐effective than alternative policies, such as simply providing targeted information on retirement planning.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: There are alternative revenue-neutral policies that could boost retirement adequacy for all.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Mr Chairman, may I have your permission to display a slide on the screen?

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira
text: CPF tax relief has retirement value because the tax savings can be used for retirement instead.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira
text: The numbers will, of course, have to be studied further.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira
text: So, my suggestions are: first, could the Ministry provide a regular update on the tax cost of the CPF and SRS tax relief system, and estimates of how effective SRS is at inducing additional retirement savings?

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira
text: Second, could the Ministry study revenue‐neutral alternatives, such as matching contribution credits to CPF, that would boost retirement adequacy for the broad middle class while increasing progressivity of the tax system?

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Chairman, the Foreign Maid Levy Relief is currently given to married, separated, divorced and widowed women with school-going children to claim relief for Foreign Domestic Worker (FDW) levy paid for domestic workers they or their husband employed in the previous year.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Singles and married men are not eligible, as are separated, divorced or widowed women with no children to claim child reliefs.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The policy objective is to encourage women to stay in the workforce.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I urge MOF to expand the scope of the levy generously to all Singaporeans who paid the foreign maid levy for domestic workers taking care of children, elderly parents or people with disabilities.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This will then encourage all caregiving Singaporeans to stay in the workforce, regardless of gender and marital status.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Furthermore, the Government has announced it would expand the scope of the FDW Grant and replace it with the Home Caregiving Grant in recognition of the sacrifices made by caregivers and to support their care work.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: A universal Caregiver Levy Relief will be better aligned with this objective.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Chairman, I declare my interest as an advisor to the taxi union and the private hire union.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Taxi drivers pay daily rental fees of mostly over $100 a day for the vehicle they rent, and operation costs have also risen.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This is before the latest diesel tax hike and potential future GST increases.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The situation is made dire because of stiff competition from private hire cars.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Today, we have only 20,000 taxis on the road.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I have raised this suggestion some years back.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Will the Ministry consider a review or waiver for the GST that is levied on the daily rental of taxis that is borne by taxi drivers?

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Finance Minister Tharman Shanmugaratnam back then had replied to my suggestion that one way is to get the taxi drivers to register for GST which would then allow them to charge customers for GST and they do the claims later.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: However, it is not a feasible solution since fares are set by their respective taxi operators.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: If waiver of GST on the daily rental of taxis through this channel is not a viable solution, perhaps the Government can consider other options so that the drivers can claim back the GST paid on the rental of the vehicle that they lease from the taxi operator.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: With 15,100 taxis running on diesel, the taxi drivers have shared with me that they may need to drive longer hours and longer distances to cover the higher diesel tax.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: That defeats the purpose of trying to cut down the use of diesel.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: But because of the cost increase and you cannot pass on the cost, they need to drive longer hours.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The rental costs of hybrid taxis are also not viable.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Perhaps, in terms of the size of the MRT lines and the buses that we provided, the commuting size did not grow as much as for taxis and private hire cars.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: One way I mentioned earlier during my Budget Debate speech is to encourage operators to reduce rental for hybrid taxis or find a better booking system that reduces empty cruising for the taxi drivers or perhaps even consider reducing the pump price at their pump stations so that taxi drivers can manage the increase in diesel tax.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I hope the Government agencies that issue operating licences to them or give permits to them to operate will ensure that everyone, not just the taxi drivers, and the Government co-share the burden of diesel-generated pollution.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Even private hire drivers have told me that they are also in this dilemma because some of them use diesel vehicles.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I hope that the licensing authority like the Land Transport Authority (LTA) can track what is the size of the diesel fleet under private hire services.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Perhaps, we should have no new private hire cars that use diesel vehicles because that is not going to help us solve the problem but increases the size of the problem.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Mr Chairman, we all know how rigid most corporations are when they spend money, especially on big ticket items.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I know MOF, too, has its process in place where they would ask Government Ministries to justify their spending.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The process may be robust in seeking justification from Ministries seeking budget allocations, but how much deeper is the process so as to ensure that Government fund is well-spent, especially on big ticket items, such as on information technology (IT), and on various research and development (R&D) projects?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This is especially in the case of IT projects where the innovations are making such rapid progress that even as we put an order for one equipment, a newer and improved version is in the making.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: And by the time we install the equipment, it would before long be outdated.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: So, may I ask how does the evaluation process address this issue?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: How do we know that the funds are spent effectively and efficiently?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It is not uncommon, especially in IT, to find compatibility of equipment or programmes becomes an issue at some point if there is no proper planning.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Next, what is the impact on our workforce?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: If I may borrow the thoughts of the late economist Sir Anthony Atkinson, he pointed out that the direction of technological change should be an explicit concern of policymakers.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It should encourage innovation in a form that increases the employability of workers.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Next, I would like to touch on Government support for research projects.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In the US, the federal government played a key role in the development of iPhone and many other technological breakthroughs like global positioning systems (GPS), multi-touch screens, liquid crystal displays (LCDs) and so on.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I know research can be a bottomless pit and, at the end of the day, it may end up in the bin because the outcomes are not what were expected.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa
text: We are seeing more new‐to‐economy activities that have also been developed in recent years, such as the proliferation of financial technologies (fintechs), deep tech ventures, sharing economy apps and others.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa
text: While we continue to strengthen the ecosystem for startups to flourish, we are also encouraging smaller enterprises to innovate and to scale up.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa
text: Government policies, regulations and processes must, therefore, also keep up with the changes and stay abreast with the new business landscape.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa
text: On this note, I would like to ask MOF three questions.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa
text: For example, can the Government consider allowing companies to conduct electronic or virtual annual general meetings (AGMs) to help them save costs?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa
text: Some of the businesses may be still less tax savvy and may still require some more support.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Chairman, it is important for the Government to achieve value for money in purchases, especially in the face of anticipated rising public expenditure.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: First, large projects, especially infrastructure projects, have a long tail to their project life.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: We are at the cusp of funding some truly large infrastructure projects and adjusting reducing manpower intensity of our economy.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Therefore, I suggest that various Government agencies, when the need arises, be able to tap on even more industry experts to achieve excellent design and savings.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: At the same time, given the Government's role as one of the largest procurers of services, it can play the role of supporting innovation and enterprises, including from startups, which will benefit both citizens as consumers of these services, as well as the overall economy.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Therefore, it is important for the Government to be able to manage the balance between innovation and enterprise versus value for money.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Mr Chairman, I thank the Members for their questions and comments for MOF.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: First, fiscal sustainability, investment and other tax-related measures.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Second, how to ensure that resources are employed efficiently and effectively.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Third, our plans to strengthen support for businesses.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: I will address the cuts in the first topic and Minister Indranee will take the remaining two topics.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Mr Liang Eng Hwa and Ms Foo Mee Har asked how the Government ensures sustainability in our spending and resilience in our revenue streams.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We ensure long-term fiscal sustainability in a few ways.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: First, the Government continues to spend within its means, so as to achieve a balanced Budget over the medium term.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Second, we remain prudent in our spending and emphasise value for money in every programme.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: For development projects, especially the major ones, we have robust processes to scrutinise and ensure that they are prudently managed.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Even so, we are able to deliver good outcomes in many areas, such as healthcare, education, home ownership and public safety.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Third, we have and will continue to manage expenditure growth carefully, precisely because of concerns that Mr Liang Eng Hwa highlighted on this rise in Government expenditure.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: In fact, we have tightened Government spending in recent years, by permanently reducing the budget caps of all Ministries and Organs of State by 2% from financial year (FY) 2017 and reducing the growth in Ministries' annual budgets from FY2019.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Even as we continue with these best efforts to manage our spending, we recognise that our needs will continue to grow, particularly in healthcare, security and infrastructure, as the Finance Minister explained earlier today.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: This is close to what we collect from GST today.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: And over the next decade, we have projected that annual healthcare spending will increase by nearly 0.8 percentage points of GDP to around 3% of GDP.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We will also be spending more in areas like security and preschool education.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: So, overall, there is no doubt that our recurrent spending, despite our best efforts to manage expenditure, will continue to rise.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: This is precisely why we need to ensure a diverse and resilient revenue base to meet these growing needs.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: And I share Mr Liang Eng Hwa and Ms Foo Mee Har's concerns that we really need to ensure resilient revenues, adequate revenues, to fund these recurrent expenditures and not rely too much on NIRC.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Overall, our revenue base is a diversified one, and we are mindful not to be over-reliant on any single source.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Even as the share of NIRC has grown over the last decade, we have taken steps to ensure and enhance the resilience of other revenue streams.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: First, we keep GST broad-based while providing targeted help to lower- and middle-income households through GST Vouchers and other forms of transfers.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: In the recent Budgets, we introduced GST for imported services and revised the import GST relief limits for travellers to ensure that our GST base remains resilient with digitalisation and increasing travel.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Second, we have been looking at other possible streams of revenues, as Ms Foo Mee Har highlighted.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We looked across all possible streams, and we have increased the tax rates for personal income tax, property tax and stamp duty in recent years.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We have been careful to do so in a manner that ensures our overall system is fair and equitable, while keeping watch over our competitiveness.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: For example, today, about half of our workers pay personal income tax and the top 10% of the taxpayers contribute 80% of our personal income tax.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Around 40% of companies assessed by the Inland Revenue Authority of Singapore (IRAS) pay corporate tax and around 10% of these companies pay about 95% of our corporate income tax.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: And we will continue to ensure that we have such a system, including one with a diversified base of operating revenues, while at the same time borrowing prudently for major infrastructure projects.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: I think this is the best way to ensure we have a resilient system and also one where we can have maximum flexibility to deal with contingencies like a slowdown or a recession, as Mr Liang Eng Hwa had highlighted.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Ultimately, and most importantly, sustainable Government finances depend on whether we have a healthy and growing economy.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: With a strong economy, we will have more resources to create jobs for Singaporeans and to meet the needs of our people.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: This is the key way to grow our revenues sustainably.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Next, Mr Pritam Singh highlighted the performance of GIC and asked for more information on GIC's investments.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The mandate that the Government has given GIC is to achieve good long-term returns in order to preserve and enhance the international purchasing power of the Reserves that GIC manages.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Consistent with this mandate, GIC’s portfolio performance is evaluated not just on the returns within a single year, but on a continuing basis over the long term.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: In particular, we look at the annualised rolling 20-year real rate of return of its portfolio, which GIC publishes every year.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: This 20-year return in recent years has been lower than that in previous years.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Mr Pritam Singh has highlighted this and also highlighted the explanation that GIC has put out for this decline in the 20-year return, which is, firstly, because the high returns earned in the run-up of the tech bubble in the late 1990s have dropped out of the past 20-year period, while the subsequent bursting of the bubble and decline in asset values has remained within the 20-year window.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The second reason is that the investment environment in recent years has become more difficult, and that is so not just for GIC but for fund managers everywhere.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Nevertheless, in these challenging market conditions, GIC has done creditably.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: It has continued to generate positive returns on its portfolio.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: What I have explained is published in the GIC annual report.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Every year's annual report includes an extensive write-up on how GIC manages the portfolio, including its investment methodology and risk management framework.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: While the relevant measure for its long-term mandate is the rolling 20-year return, which I just highlighted, GIC has also been putting out more information in its annual report.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: For example, it publishes other indicators, including its rolling 10-year and five-year nominal returns, and how they compare against a typical market portfolio adopted by large global investors.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Mr Pritam Singh would like even more short-term indicators; he has asked for annual indicators.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: But it is well accepted in the investment world that a requirement to report short-term performance leads to short-term investment behaviour by fund managers.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: And this is especially important because market booms and downturns are a common feature of global markets.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: For example, if there is a market downturn, a short-term investor will try to unwind its holdings to cut losses so as to limit the damage to its short-term performance.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: By contrast, a long-term investor will be able to look at fundamental valuations and ride through short-term market cycles so as to achieve better long-term returns.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: This is, in fact, a major strength that GIC has, and it is important that we continue to preserve this long-term orientation.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: If GIC puts out annual indicators, there is the inevitable risk that this will incentivise its fund managers to be more mindful of short-term investment outcomes.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: And I think this will weaken and undermine GIC's strategic advantage as a long-term endowment fund.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: I should also clarify that while GIC reveals its past performance over five-, 10- and 20-year periods, this is categorically not the basis for estimating its future performance.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: As the Government has explained several times before in this House, including when the Constitution was amended for the NIRC framework, the process of estimating the long-term expected returns of GIC, as well as that of MAS and Temasek, rests on thorough professional assessments of the future investment environment.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The Government then proposes these long-term expected return rates to the President, who does a further independent check, as advised by the Council of Presidential Advisors.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: So, there is a robust system in place to determine and evaluate the long-term expected returns.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: And as we have explained in this House, and the GIC's Annual Report also highlighted, there are reasons to expect a weakening of investment returns for serious, diversified global investors over the next 20 years compared to the past, and this is due to structural headwinds in the external environment, for example, demographics, elevated debt and lower productivity in many countries.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira asked about CPF and SRS tax reliefs.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We do have a range of policies to address the retirement adequacy needs of different groups.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Currently, SRS and CPF contributions are exempted from tax, subject to certain conditions, and the tax exemption is meant to encourage people to save for their own retirement.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: I know Assoc Prof Theseira has highlighted some international studies.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: In keeping with progressivity, the Government limits the tax benefits that higher income individuals receive from CPF and SRS.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: For CPF, there is a salary ceiling and top-up limits that restrict the amount of contributions to the system and, consequently, the amount of relief claimable.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: For SRS, there is an annual cap on contributions.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The SRS is a tax deferral scheme, and not fully tax-exempt like the CPF.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: So, overall, our system of taxes and transfers remains progressive.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: I do share Assoc Prof Theseira's objective of having a fair and equitable system to improve retirement adequacy for all Singaporeans.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: So, we will continue to review our schemes, taking in suggestions and feedback and ensure that the balance of support remains tilted towards the lower- and middle-income groups.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh asked about the foreign maid levy relief.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: As he highlighted, this relief is quite specific, with an objective of encouraging women to stay in the workforce after marriage and child birth.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: He asked about broader support and, indeed, we do have a range of broad-based schemes in place today to support caregiving.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: There are similar tax reliefs of up to $4,000 per child or $7,500 per handicapped child for those who care for their dependent children.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: For these reliefs, the family has the flexibility to decide on the care arrangements for the child or elderly parent, which may not necessarily involve the hiring of an FDW.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The tax reliefs for the care of dependent children and aged parents, and the concessionary FDW levy, are not dependent on the gender of the caregiver.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: So, these support measures are also on top of existing subsidies to the care recipient, such as subsidised healthcare.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Basically, we do want to do more to support caregivers and we will continue to review our policies regularly to ensure their relevance and effectiveness.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Mr Ang Hin Kee asked about GST waiver for taxi rentals.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Singapore adopts a broad-based GST regime with few exemptions, and we chose this approach to keep our GST rate relatively low and administration simple.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Nevertheless, we will certainly do whatever we can to help taxi drivers and private hire car (PHC) drivers better manage their businesses as well as their regulatory compliance costs.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: For example, last year, after a review with the National Private Hire Vehicles Association and the Ministry of Transport (MOT), MOF amended the Income Tax Act to allow private hire car drivers to claim tax deductions for motor car-related expenses like car rental and petrol against their driving income for income tax purposes.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Taxi drivers are already entitled to this, but we extended it to private hire car drivers.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: This percentage was decided after an extensive public consultation by MOF.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: And drivers, of course, can opt to claim tax deductions based on actual expenses incurred if their expenses exceed 60%.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: I hear Mr Ang Hin Kee, who has suggested raising the 60% to a higher figure, but we have had extensive consultations and we have arrived at this figure just very recently.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: MOF will continue to monitor and review and update the figure if and when necessary.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: With regard to diesel duties, we have explained the need for this restructuring of the diesel regime from ownership to usage-based taxes which is necessary for a cleaner environment and better health.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Besides the restructuring of diesel taxes, we also have a range of measures to encourage the shift towards cleaner vehicles, and taxi operators are, indeed, responding.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We have seen strong growth in the number of cleaner taxis, and we now have more than 5,000 electric and hybrid taxis plying our roads, or about 30% of the entire taxi population.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: To cushion the impact of the increase in diesel duties, we have provided some measures to help users, including taxi drivers, manage the transition.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: As Mr Ang Hin Kee is aware, the Government has been working with taxi companies to encourage them to pass down the savings from the Special Tax reduction to their drivers.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: And I am glad that all taxi companies have agreed to do so.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Mr Ang had many other suggestions to work with companies and to help the drivers, including through licensing or through the pump prices that the companies offer.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We will study these suggestions and will continue to work with the taxi operators to see how best to improve the welfare of drivers.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Mr Chairman, let me conclude by reaffirming MOF’s commitment to ensuring the long-term sustainability of our fiscal system.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We will continue to build a resilient and progressive tax and benefit regime to support our rising spending needs.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: I will let Minister Indranee address the other questions that have been raised.

speaker: The Minister in the Prime Minister's Office, Second Minister for Education and Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Mr Chairman, let me now address Members' questions on how the Government manages our spending and how we support businesses.

speaker: The Minister in the Prime Minister's Office, Second Minister for Education and Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Ms Foo Mee Har and Mr Saktiandi Supaat asked how the Government manages our infrastructure and info-communications technology (ICT) spending in the long run, and how we ensure that these programmes deliver value to citizens and businesses.

speaker: The Minister in the Prime Minister's Office, Second Minister for Education and Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: On average, we expect that development expenditure will increase in the coming decade as we continue to invest in public infrastructure and adopt ICT to meet citizens’ needs and support our economy.

speaker: The Minister in the Prime Minister's Office, Second Minister for Education and Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: We, therefore, place significant emphasis on identifying opportunities for cost savings and achieving better outcomes in these areas.

speaker: The Minister in the Prime Minister's Office, Second Minister for Education and Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Before we embark on a project, there is a robust process to consult stakeholders and assess the need for the project, the broad scope and timeline, and the balance of benefits over costs.

speaker: The Minister in the Prime Minister's Office, Second Minister for Education and Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: For a major project like the Changi East development, the Cabinet must first be satisfied of the need for the project before it can proceed further.

speaker: The Minister in the Prime Minister's Office, Second Minister for Education and Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: We also conduct public consultations on our future infrastructure plans, such as the Urban Redevelopment Authority (URA) Master Plan and the Land Transport Masterplan.

speaker: The Minister in the Prime Minister's Office, Second Minister for Education and Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: All public infrastructure projects above $100 million are also carefully reviewed by a team of architects and engineers within MOF, before approval is granted by the Development Planning Committee (DPC) comprising three Cabinet Ministers.

speaker: The Minister in the Prime Minister's Office, Second Minister for Education and Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Projects above $500 million are put through the Gateway process, where they are subject to additional scrutiny by the Development Projects Advisory Panel that includes senior public officers, academics and industry practitioners with deep technical expertise.

speaker: The Minister in the Prime Minister's Office, Second Minister for Education and Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: In one review, the design for an MRT station was improved such that two proposed underground links and entrances could be brought to ground level, yet without compromising the objectives of commuter accessibility and connectivity.

speaker: The Minister in the Prime Minister's Office, Second Minister for Education and Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: This redesign reduced the amount of utility diversions, underground excavation and tunnelling works required, leading to an estimated cost savings of $54 million.

speaker: The Minister in the Prime Minister's Office, Second Minister for Education and Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: All major Government ICT projects are reviewed by a committee of experienced public sector officers and ICT practitioners before approval.

speaker: The Minister in the Prime Minister's Office, Second Minister for Education and Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Besides reviewing projects before granting approval, the Government also monitors existing services and programmes post-implementation.

speaker: The Minister in the Prime Minister's Office, Second Minister for Education and Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: We actively seek ways to enhance cost-efficiency and outcomes.

speaker: The Minister in the Prime Minister's Office, Second Minister for Education and Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Improvements can arise by leveraging technology, improving processes and collaborating across agencies.

speaker: The Minister in the Prime Minister's Office, Second Minister for Education and Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: For example, the National Library Board now uses robots and automatic sorting machines to help staff and volunteers with shelving work.

speaker: The Minister in the Prime Minister's Office, Second Minister for Education and Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Library users can also check out books without queuing by using a mobile app, and pick up reserved items at self-service lockers outside library operating hours.

speaker: The Minister in the Prime Minister's Office, Second Minister for Education and Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: These have helped to achieve cost savings of $2 million annually, in addition to bringing convenience to citizens.

speaker: The Minister in the Prime Minister's Office, Second Minister for Education and Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Agencies also tap on one another's expertise to co-develop and co-deliver programmes that bring about better outcomes for citizens.

speaker: The Minister in the Prime Minister's Office, Second Minister for Education and Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: For example, the Public Service Division (PSD) mentioned in its Committee of Supply (COS) that agencies at Our Tampines Hub (OTH) will be coming together to cross-train counter staff for better service to citizens.

speaker: The Minister in the Prime Minister's Office, Second Minister for Education and Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Besides counter services, the People's Association, Sport Singapore and the Health Promotion Board are also collaborating on joint programming opportunities at OTH.

speaker: The Minister in the Prime Minister's Office, Second Minister for Education and Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Just last Sunday, they organised "The Greater Singapore Workout" for more than 200 participants of all ages, achieving community bonding and healthy lifestyle promotion objectives simultaneously.

speaker: The Minister in the Prime Minister's Office, Second Minister for Education and Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Such efforts are bearing fruit, with agencies seeking ways to achieve greater value-for-money in their work.

speaker: The Minister in the Prime Minister's Office, Second Minister for Education and Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Residents experienced less inconvenience as construction time was shortened by two months, and this also generated cost savings of about $3.6 million.

speaker: The Minister in the Prime Minister's Office, Second Minister for Education and Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Such collaboration between public agencies and citizens is a good example of partnership at work.

speaker: The Minister in the Prime Minister's Office, Second Minister for Education and Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Value-for-money lessons learnt from one agency are shared across the Public Service so that they can be applied by others.

speaker: The Minister in the Prime Minister's Office, Second Minister for Education and Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: MOF also guides agencies in applying different methodologies to quantify costs and benefits of their programmes, and setting outcome-based indicators to monitor their effectiveness.

speaker: The Minister in the Prime Minister's Office, Second Minister for Education and Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Mr Henry Kwek and Mr Liang Eng Hwa asked how Government procurement policies support innovation and enterprise, in addition to ensuring value-for-money in Government spending.

speaker: The Minister in the Prime Minister's Office, Second Minister for Education and Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Achieving value for money remains an important criterion in Government procurement decisions, but it does not mean awarding contracts only to the lowest quote.

speaker: The Minister in the Prime Minister's Office, Second Minister for Education and Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The Government has adopted price-quality evaluation as the default approach in tenders, where a balance of price and quality factors are considered.

speaker: The Minister in the Prime Minister's Office, Second Minister for Education and Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Today, about half of Government tenders are not awarded to the lowest bidder.

speaker: The Minister in the Prime Minister's Office, Second Minister for Education and Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The Government has also stepped up the adoption of more outcome-based procurement, where tenderers have more flexibility to propose innovative solutions to meet the desired outcomes.

speaker: The Minister in the Prime Minister's Office, Second Minister for Education and Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: For example, JTC adopted an outcome-based security contract for one of its business parks.

speaker: The Minister in the Prime Minister's Office, Second Minister for Education and Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Apart from being open to good ideas and solutions, we also continually seek to make it easier for small and medium enterprises (SMEs) to participate in Government procurement.

speaker: The Minister in the Prime Minister's Office, Second Minister for Education and Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: We now accept unaudited financial statements if the company's Director certifies that their financial statements are accurate and true.

speaker: The Minister in the Prime Minister's Office, Second Minister for Education and Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Smaller companies and startups without GSR can capture higher-value Government projects through Quotations, which come with simpler contractual terms and conditions and tend to be processed more quickly.

speaker: The Minister in the Prime Minister's Office, Second Minister for Education and Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: We hope that many among the 12,000 suppliers who participate in Quotations but not Tenders will benefit from this.

speaker: The Minister in the Prime Minister's Office, Second Minister for Education and Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: I agree with Mr Henry Kwek and Mr Liang Eng Hwa that the key here is balance.

speaker: The Minister in the Prime Minister's Office, Second Minister for Education and Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Government procurement can help to give a boost but, fundamentally, for companies to grow and be competitive, they must be innovative and offer value-for-money solutions.

speaker: The Minister in the Prime Minister's Office, Second Minister for Education and Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Mr Liang Eng Hwa asked how the Government taps on digital technology to streamline corporate regulatory requirements.

speaker: The Minister in the Prime Minister's Office, Second Minister for Education and Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The Government has continued to simplify and digitise corporate regulations.

speaker: The Minister in the Prime Minister's Office, Second Minister for Education and Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Over the past two years, a number of improvements have been made.

speaker: The Minister in the Prime Minister's Office, Second Minister for Education and Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: We reduced the number of steps in the annual returns filing form for eligible companies.

speaker: The Minister in the Prime Minister's Office, Second Minister for Education and Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The simplified form is available on the Accounting and Corporate Regulatory Authority's (ACRA's) mobile app and the online BizFile+ portal.

speaker: The Minister in the Prime Minister's Office, Second Minister for Education and Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Company directors and secretaries can receive short message service (SMS) reminders to file their annual returns and meet statutory obligations on behalf of their companies.

speaker: The Minister in the Prime Minister's Office, Second Minister for Education and Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Mr Liang Eng Hwa's suggestion on virtual AGMs is a good one.

speaker: The Minister in the Prime Minister's Office, Second Minister for Education and Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Mr Liang Eng Hwa also asked how the Government can help small enterprises and freelancers understand their statutory obligations.

speaker: The Minister in the Prime Minister's Office, Second Minister for Education and Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: ACRA's Directors Training Programme has helped new and aspiring company directors understand their statutory obligations under the Companies Act.

speaker: The Minister in the Prime Minister's Office, Second Minister for Education and Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: In April 2018, ACRA worked with CPF Board, Enterprise SG, IRAS, the Ministry of Manpower (MOM) and the Singapore Institute of Directors to provide an online training programme for directors.

speaker: The Minister in the Prime Minister's Office, Second Minister for Education and Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Company directors can access the online programme anytime, anywhere, and more than 2,500 have done so since its launch.

speaker: The Minister in the Prime Minister's Office, Second Minister for Education and Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: We have received positive feedback that the programme has helped company directors better understand their roles and responsibilities.

speaker: The Minister in the Prime Minister's Office, Second Minister for Education and Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Some businesses may prefer to receive help in person.

speaker: The Minister in the Prime Minister's Office, Second Minister for Education and Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The Taxpayer and Business Service Centre located in Revenue House offers businesses one-stop Government services by co-locating taxpayer services.

speaker: The Minister in the Prime Minister's Office, Second Minister for Education and Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Mr Chairman, as I have just a little bit more, may I seek your indulgence for a couple more minutes?

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: As I was saying, the Taxpayer and Business Service Centre co-locates taxpayer services, CorpPass, ACRA and Enterprise Singapore services.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Businesses can meet staff from ACRA, IRAS, Enterprise Singapore SME Centre and CorpPass there for help with their questions about regulations and tax obligations, amongst other issues.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We support research, development and innovation through different schemes where we also require co-payment in order to keep them relevant.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: On the Government side, where the innovation has a long horizon, are higher-risk or involve manpower development like PhD training, then the Government takes a bigger role.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: In R&D, we invest in areas that support current and future competitiveness, like digital technology, advanced manufacturing, urban solutions and sustainability, and health and medical solutions.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We will continue to partner citizens, businesses and the community to achieve good outcomes with the resources entrusted to us.

speaker: The Chairman
text: We have a bit of time for clarification.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee
text: I can sense that Mr Lawrence Wong understands the plight that the taxi drivers are facing.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee
text: Unlike many countries where the digital disruption of Uber and Grab has caused a lot of chaos and there were strikes, fights and the burning of vehicles – even taxi drivers in some countries burn themselves to death just to show their protest – ours have been relatively supportive and they have seen the advent of technological disruption and tried to accommodate, everybody trying to make a living on the road.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee
text: We have 65,000 taxis and private hires on the road, and only about 1.2 million-plus commuting traffic a day, which is less than 100% of the increase in the vehicle fleet size.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee
text: I think the market probably cannot absorb so many vehicles.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee
text: So, despite the diesel tax, there is really not a big market and we have many vehicles, and every driver trying to eke out a little living from this.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee
text: Perhaps, the Ministry can consider that we may not need such a big size of vehicles on the road because it is not just technology; it is just the size of the market that is not big enough to accommodate —

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Ang Hin Kee, can you keep your clarifications short?

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee
text: So, I would like to ask the Minister if MOF would look at this kind of parameters rather than only on diesel tax as a way to manage the vehicles on the road.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Mr Chairman, I can confirm to Mr Ang Hin Kee that it is not just a sense.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: I do share and understand what the drivers have to go through.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: That is why MOF works very closely with the private hire car drivers and the taxi drivers earlier on when we amended the Income Tax Act to allow for deductions and for it to be done on a deemed expense basis.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, as I have said, there are many ways in which we can look at this.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Not all of the levers are with the Government.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Taxi companies and operators can do their part, too, as Mr Ang Hin Kee has suggested.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, the Government will continue to work with the companies, the associations and the unions to see how best we can help our drivers who are impacted.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira
text: Because the international studies show that much of the response actually comes from this kind of diversion – movement from the taxed to the untaxed account.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: Mr Chairman, I would like to ask a clarification from Minister Indranee Rajah.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: With regard to the Government's expenditure on infrastructure projects and also IT spending, I firmly believe that Government spending plays a big role in terms of giving direction in terms of technological change in the long run and also it is an explicit concern for policymakers.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: So, my question is about balancing the value-for-money and cost-savings that the Minister mentioned and the outcomes.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: The Minister mentioned about the outcomes and my clarification is whether the issue of employability of workers in the long run is part of the outcomes as well, rather than in terms of what the Minister mentioned just now, of public sector concerns in terms of outcomes as another option or parameter.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: But in terms of outcomes, what is the Minister's definition of outcomes?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: Does it involve in the long run the impact on work, workers or jobs lost or gained?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: So, it is a clarification on that point.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: When we look at outcomes, we look at a variety of things.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Obviously, we want to look at efficiency, we want to make sure, depending on the project, reliability.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: If the question is: will we look solely at one factor, for example, "Does this result in employment of a certain group?", it cannot be seen in isolation.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, where we can, we try to encourage businesses to employ.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: But that is really done through the work of MOM and it cannot be a single type of factor driving the way that project requirements are structured, because then you might have all sorts of other unintended outcomes.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa
text: Given the consumption rate and so on, is the $8 billion that was set aside ahead of utilisation or are we still in good shape in terms of the funding for the whole Pioneer Generation Package?

speaker: The Chairman
text: In light of the surplus that we have, is the hon Member given leave to withdraw the amendment?
